paras: The Bill Walker manhunt was the pursuit of Bill Walker, a Black man, by sheriff's posses in Mobile County, Alabama, beginning July 31, 1910, after he was accused of assaulting a white woman at Axis and killing a Black man. Wire services reported on August 1 that a mob had shot him to death and burned his body. Mobile dispatches showed instead that he escaped posse gunfire, was arrested in Mississippi, guarded in jail against lynching, and convicted of murder on September 8.

Axis was a mill town on the Southern Railway about eighteen miles north of Mobile. According to the Montgomery Advertiser's Mobile correspondent, a Black man lured Mrs. J. O. Gibson from her home soon after 1 a.m. on Sunday, July 31, attacked her in the woods, cut her throat and hands, and slashed her eight-year-old brother, Clarence Howell. The assailant, named as Bill Walker, then shot Jesse Brown, a Black man, through his window and forced Brown's wife, Katie, to go with him.

Sheriff John S. Drago organized posses at Axis, and the Advertiser reported that 'irate citizens' in the search would lynch Walker if they caught him before the officers did. That night Walker took Katie Brown to the water tank at Cold Creek station and tried to board a train carrying posse members, who opened fire. Katie Brown escaped and could not say what became of Walker, and at midnight a telephone message from Axis said he had 'undoubtedly been shot or lynched by a posse.'

Later Mobile reports said Walker had escaped because the train's fireman fired before the posse could surround him. Bloodhounds lost his trail, the county Board of Revenue gave the sheriff $100 for the hunt, and by August 2 about fifty deputies were searching with the roads guarded.

Walker was arrested at Benndale, Mississippi, and on August 10 Mrs. Gibson picked him out of a row of cells at the Mobile jail. He denied the assault but admitted killing Jesse Brown. The sheriff kept a double armed guard on the jail, and Judge O. J. Semmes called a special court term because 'hostile sentiment was freely expressed.'

On August 21 Arthur Neill, a Black man held at the Vinegar Bend stockade for vagrancy, reportedly confessed to the assault on Mrs. Gibson and said Walker had killed Brown. Amid 'strong talk of a lynching' at Vinegar Bend, deputies who saw a mob forming took Neill to Mobile on a freight train. After hearing Neill's confession, Mrs. Gibson said she could not see how it could be anybody else.

A special grand jury indicted Walker on three charges, and Judge Semmes refused a change of venue. On September 8 a jury deliberated fifteen minutes and convicted him of first-degree murder with a recommendation of death, after he testified that he had fired into the Brown house meaning to kill Katie Brown. The assault charges were not tried, and no report of his sentencing was found.

The false lynching report ran on August 1 from Detroit to El Paso under headlines such as 'Negro Is Shot To Death and Burned' and 'VENGEANCE IS SWIFT'. Its datelines placed the town at 'Alexis' in Alabama, Louisiana or Georgia, and the East Oregonian ran it as 'Lynching in Louisiana' beside the Slocum, Texas, killings. The story kept circulating after Walker was reported alive; on August 6 the Alaska Citizen said a crowd 'dealt out rough justice to the coon.'

The Montgomery Advertiser's first report called the assailant a 'negro brute' and carried the deck 'MOB METES QUICK JUSTICE', though its text left Walker's fate open. Its later dispatches, and the Birmingham Age-Herald's, followed the jail guard, Neill's confession and the trial without comment; no coverage of the case was found in the Black press. A Pensacola Journal reader's letter cited 'the man hunt going on now around Mobile' as an example of lynching it blamed on Black crime.

The later, local Mobile reports contradict the wire lynching story, which echoes the midnight 'shot or lynched' message. The identity of Mrs. Gibson's assailant was also disputed: she identified Walker on August 10, but Neill later confessed with details she said matched.

reader.title: Bill Walker manhunt and false lynching report
bases: A posse fired on Bill Walker during a manhunt and citizens were said to intend to lynch him, and wire stories reported him shot and burned by a mob, but Alabama papers showed him alive, jailed under guard against lynching, and tried (A1, A21, A3, A31, A45); a threatened, not completed, lynching.

Wire reports that a mob shot and burned Walker (A3, A8, A9) were contradicted by Mobile reports of an ongoing hunt, his jailing, indictment and conviction (A21, A28, A31, A42, A45); the only violence against him reported locally was posse and fireman gunfire at Cold Creek with no wound reported (A1, A21).

Early wire reports said Walker was lynched (A3, A4, A8, A9, A30), while Mobile correspondents reported his fate unknown, then his flight, arrest, identification and trial (A1, A2, A21, A31, A32, A45).

accounts.gist: A telephone report said Walker had 'undoubtedly been shot or lynched' after a posse on a train fired at him at Cold Creek, but Katie Brown could not say what became of him.

framing.detail: The Montgomery Advertiser headed its first report 'WOMAN VICTIM OF BLACK FIEND' and 'MOB METES QUICK JUSTICE' although its text said only that Walker's fate was unknown.
Northern and western papers ran the lynching wire under 'Negro Is Shot To Death and Burned', 'VENGEANCE IS SWIFT', 'NEGRO MURDERER HANDLED BY MOB' and 'Lynching in Louisiana'.
The Alaska Citizen said the crowd 'dealt out rough justice to the coon'.
Later Alabama dispatches reported the jail guard, identifications, Neill's confession and the trial without editorial comment, while still calling the crime 'horrible'.
A Pensacola Journal reader letter cited 'The man hunt going on now around Mobile' as an instance of lynching it attributed to Black crime, and called for federal 'expulsion'.
